content: Methylendioxypyrovalerone (MDPV), also referred to as MDPK or 1-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-2-pyrrolidinyl-pentan-1-one, is a stimulant drug that functions as a norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor. It is reported to have approximately four times the potency of methylphenidate. This compound has been used recreationally as a stimulant and aphrodisiac, often categorized as a designer drug. MDPV typically appears as an off-white to light-brown, crumbly powder that is highly hydrophilic. When exposed to air for extended periods, it darkens slightly in color and develops an odor reminiscent of potato tubers. This odor has been attributed to the presence of pyrrolidine as an impurity. The substance is known to degrade rapidly and lose potency when dissolved in solution. The subjective effects of MDPV include central nervous system stimulation, euphoria, hypersexuality, agitation or anxiety, and insomnia. These effects generally last between three to six hours. At higher doses, MDPV has been observed to cause intense and prolonged anxiety attacks, particularly in individuals who are intolerant to stimulants. Anecdotal reports suggest that higher doses or frequent dosing intervals may lead to addiction. MDPV has been noted for its aphrodisiac properties, which some users claim rival those of methamphetamine when dosed appropriately. However, its general effects are reportedly less potent than methamphetamine, and it may pose a lower risk of harm, as there have been no documented cases of death or severe disability associated with its abuse in online forums dedicated to research chemicals. Structurally, MDPV is the 3,4-methylenedioxy ring-substituted analogue of the appetite suppressant pyrovalerone. Despite its structural similarity to other methylenedioxyphenylalkylamine derivatives like MDMA and methylone, MDPV produces purely stimulant effects without any empathogenic qualities. Prolonged use or binges of MDPV have been associated with severe withdrawal symptoms, including depression, lethargy, and headaches, similar to the come-down syndrome experienced with methamphetamine. MDPV is not explicitly classified as an illegal drug in any country. However, its structural similarity to controlled substances suggests that it may be considered a controlled substance analogue in countries such as the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. Other analogues derived from alpha-pyrrolidinopropiophenone include the 4-methyl analogue pyrovalerone, as well as analogues with no substitutions on the aromatic ring or with alkyl chains containing three to six carbons. These compounds have been reported as stimulants of abuse, primarily in Germany and other European countries, since the early 2000s. Despite this, they remain relatively obscure and are rarely encountered by law enforcement. MDPV was never widely sold online in large quantities and, as of October 2007, has become virtually unobtainable.
